We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking.

Kimi K3 is so massive that it needs 16x B200s across two NVIDIA servers, but it fits inside one 8x MI355X AMD server because AMD gives you much more HBM memory per GPU. That single AMD node hit: - 952 tok/s total throughput - 118 tok/s for a single user - Nearly 4x the throughput per node of the 16× B200 setup - Better performance per dollar than both B200 and B300 But the craziest part is that ROCm mostly worked out of the box. @wafer_ai only had to make a few relatively small fixes. No months of kernel engineering. No custom kernels at all. Even the slow time-to-first-token problem came down mostly to one attention kernel not loading because Kimi had 12 heads instead of a supported shape. They simply padded 12 to 16, used AMD’s fast existing kernel, and cut cold-prefill time by roughly 2–3x AMD’s bet on packing more HBM into each server is going to become extremely important as frontier open models keep getting larger. If AMD keeps improving ROCm and day-one model support, data-center operators will have to seriously consider these GPUs. The CUDA moat isn’t dead yet, but this definitely puts a big dent in it.

CJ Stroud before the draft came out of Ohio State and scored 18 out of 100 on the S2 cognition test which is basically an exam that NFL teams use to measure how fast a quarterback processes information. Bryce Young who was picked 1 pick ahead of him scored a 98 out of 100. Stroud’s score was the lowest score of any QB coming out of that draft class. And yesterday he got mocked for a warmup that went viral with his eyes. He got mocked for his cognition test and now the internet is trolling him for working on one of the most important parts of being a QB… the brain. But what is he actually doing? The drill is called “saccades” and there is real sports science and data behind it. After looking this up and trying to keep it concise and easy to understand here is what I found. A saccade is the fast, involuntary jump your eyes make when they snap from one target to another, which is exactly what a quarterback's eyes do on every dropback as he moves from his first read to his second to his checkdown in under three seconds. Stroud holds his thumbs out and flicks his eyes between them, horizontally and then vertically, training those jumps to be faster and more controlled. It’s part of the same screening doctors use to check for a concussion, and there are vision training companies that now sell a version of this to QBs to speed up how fast they can process a defense pre snap. But what makes this all funny is three years ago the sports world decided Stroud’s processing was a weakness. Now he’s putting in the work and has turned into a meme. Now, I do understand the video is pretty funny but got to give Stroud some credit here because when he came out of Ohio State he dismissed his test score as well. Stroud is coming off a rough season that ended with four interceptions in a playoff loss to New England, and he has plenty to prove in 2026. But a QB quietly drilling the one skill that decides games, the speed of what happens in his brain, is the last thing anyone should be clowning, plus the one thing that cost Stroud in the playoffs was processing and decision making. Netflix replaced their 15 years old recommendation algorithm with an LLM.
It’s called "GenRec" and it completely changes how recommendation algorithms are built.
For over a decade, the Netflix recommendation engine was a masterclass in feature engineering. Data scientists built thousands of complex, handcrafted features to figure out what you wanted to watch next.
It required bespoke architectures. Massive infrastructure. Constant manual tuning.
Netflix threw all of it away.
They built GenRec, an LLM-backed ranker.
Instead of translating your behavior into complex math, they just turn your watch history and metadata into a natural language sentence.
They feed that raw text into a foundation LLM.
The AI simply reads your behavior like a story, understands your evolving tastes, and scores the entire catalog in a single forward pass.
No manual feature engineering. No complex bespoke architectures.
Here is the part that should terrify traditional data scientists.
This text-based LLM didn't just match the highly tuned production system Netflix spent years perfecting.
It beat it.
And it achieved those statistically significant gains using roughly 40x fewer labeled training examples.
We are watching a massive paradigm shift in real time.
The most complex predictive algorithms in the world are being replaced by models that just know how to read.

A new paper from Alexander W. Crosier examines Kalshi’s next-day weather markets.
The findings:
• Kalshi beats the most accurate public forecast, the National Blend of Models (NBM), in six of seven cities studied.
• Kalshi outperforms NBM by 10% a day ahead.
• Kalshi beats a weighted blend of public forecasts at every horizon tested: day ahead, evening before, and morning of.
From daily plans to decisions about flights, farming, and energy supply, better weather forecasts help people make better decisions.
That’s the value of price discovery on an open exchange: trading produces useful information for everyone.
How do traders improve on forecasts built by meteorologists? The paper explains:
“Traders do not need to make a better weather model than the meteorologists. They only need to start from what has been published and add anything that the weather guidance missed.”
Markets give people a financial incentive to be right. Traders build sophisticated models, analyze public forecasts, and seek out information others have missed. They compete to identify and offer better prices, incorporating that information into the market’s forecast.
The benefits extend to everyone: the resulting forecast is available to people who never place a trade. ~75% of people who use Kalshi come for the forecasts, not to trade.
The Weather Company, Fox Weather, and thousands of everyday people are using Kalshi’s weather data: markets turn competing analyses into information people can use.
Read the full paper here: arxiv.org/pdf/2609.23969

I stand by that some of the best ideas in Computer Science can be found from failed research of the late 90s.
DataScalar is no longer around, but they would have made a killing today.
They created an architecture which was, to put it simply, a memory centric execution model. You trade excess threads for reduction of data movement.
But *unlike* multithreading the way we think about it today, you’d have *redundant*, sequential programs running multiple times.
At the time, DataScalar was making the (risky!) bet that future processors would have arithmetic become virtually free compared to data movement. You deliberately waste (tons) of CPU cycles, on an otherwise unaware application, where the CPU that “wins” is whichever one happens to be closer to the memory that’s needed.
Instead of designing a better prefetcher, you just race all the threads against each other, the winner (local memory owner) one-way broadcasts, and the other cores get the result without making a conventional remote request.
Today, you’d call it…an odd form of near-data processing. What I find really interesting is in the present era most redundant processing is done in a lockstep / safety sense (aerospace, etc), not a performance / latency sensitive sense.
Weirdly, the technique isn’t that far off from the data racing I did in my TailSlayer project to reduce RAM refresh latency stalls.

Columbia professor Sandra Matz on how asking ChatGPT for ice cream 100 times, and getting the same two flavors 96 times, shows AI flattening human choice:
Matz starts by giving algorithms credit. They get so good at predicting what we want because they focus on exploitation, leaning on what already works.
"And that's not just good for business, it's also good and sometimes even necessary for us as consumers."
The reason is how many choices we face:
"For me, the mere thought of having to choose between 31 different ice cream flavors makes me dizzy. And yet, most of the choices that we face day to day are far more complex than that. Netflix, for example, has over 5,500 movies to choose from. Spotify over 100 million songs."
Her conclusion: "Without a little help from our exploitation loving AI friends, we simply don't stand a chance at navigating modern life."
But she sees a catch:
"I've also become increasingly concerned that this upside comes at a somewhat existential cost."
To show what she means, she went back to those 31 flavors. She asked ChatGPT to recommend a Baskin Robbins flavor, pretending each time to be a new customer, and repeated it 100 times.
"96 times. It recommended one of their two most popular flavors, Pralines and Cream and Mint Chocolate Chip, which I realize, and I'm sure you'd agree, is not exactly a very diverse set of choices."
Then she follows that to its logical end:
"It could mean that we soon find ourselves in a world where Baskin Robbins offers only those two flavors. If no one ever picks the other 29, why bother offering them in the first place?"
Matz admits that ice cream sounds like a trivial example. Her point is that the same thing happens everywhere else:
"This might sound trivial and not really existential at all, but that's only until you realize that this flattening of the human experience happens across every aspect of life."
Her research shows how far it goes. In studies with her collaborators and students, people who used AI for guidance showed three effects:
Their creative output became less unique.
Their preferences became more normative and less diverse.
Their picks for the most important scientists, athletes, and historical figures ended up the same as everyone else's.
@sandracmatz sums it up this way:
"AI turns this infinite diversity of human opinions, beliefs, and preferences into statistically safe sameness."

I used to be the person companies called after they got hacked.

The hack almost never sank them. The cover-up did.
Every time, the team’s instinct was the same: wait until we know more, wait until we're sure, wait until we have the perfect statement, etc.
And some of the biggest companies in the world have learned what that waiting costs.
In 2016, Uber got hacked. Instead of telling anyone, it paid the hackers $100K to delete the data and stay quiet, and labeled it a bug bounty. The truth came out a year later. Uber paid $148M to settle with all 50 states, and its former security chief was criminally convicted.
That same year, Yahoo revealed that a 2014 breach had exposed 500M accounts. The news landed in the middle of Verizon buying the company. Verizon cut $350M off the price.
And in 2017, Equifax discovered a breach affecting over 140M Americans, then waited 40 days to tell the public. During that window, an executive who'd figured out what happened sold nearly $1M in stock. He went to prison for insider trading.
Meanwhile, hackers don't wait. They post your data. They email your customers directly. And when customers hear it from a stranger first, that trust is gone for good.
Telling customers early doesn't mean admitting fault. It can be as simple as: "We found suspicious activity. We're investigating. Here's what you should do right now. We'll update you as we learn more."
On Tuesday, I'm sharing the exact framework I'd use to write that email if I were in your shoes. Follow and turn on notifications so it's there when you need it.
Customers will forgive you for getting hacked. Most of them expect it by now.

ETFs / Event indices:

We could create similar indices for real-world events like a "US Recession Index" or "AI Boom Index", combining dozen of events into a single tradable index.
